name: ebook2cw
why: Turns any ebook into Morse code audio you can listen to, a delightful transform from text into radio-style sound.

brief.what_it_is: ebook2cw is a command-line program that converts a plain text file (ASCII, ISO 8859-1, or UTF-8), such as an ebook, into Morse code audio in MP3 or OGG format. You pass it the text file and options for speed, tone frequency, waveform, chapter splitting, and ID3 tags, and it writes audio files. A separate GUI, ebook2cwgui, is optional. The page lists Windows, Linux, FreeBSD and Mac OS X as supported platforms.
brief.why_it_exists: The author, Fabian Kurz (DJ5CW, ex DJ1YFK), wrote it so anyone can make a CW audio book to their own liking. He says earlier hams had made Morse audiobooks, but distributing them as finished audio files limited flexibility and needed a lot of bandwidth.
brief.how_it_works: The program reads the text and turns each character into Morse using built-in code tables (ISO 8859-1 by default, UTF-8 with -u). Inline text commands such as |f400, |w60 and |S1000 change tone, speed, or insert silence mid-text, and prosigns can be written in angle brackets like <AR>. Output is split into numbered files at chapter markers or by duration or word count. Settings can also be stored in an ebook2cw.conf file.

commands_seen.context: Windows example from the Usage section: converts Book.txt at 40 wpm, splitting chapters at the word Chapter and writing Book-0000.mp3, Book-0001.mp3, and so on.
Performance section: suggested settings (sample rate 22050, MP3 bitrate 32) if an MP3 player fails on the default settings.
Build target that compiles ebook2cw to run as a CGI program on a web server.
Alternative build target for the CGI version.
Example CGI request that returns a sound file saying hello world at 25 wpm character speed, 20 wpm effective speed, 600 Hz.
Sets CW speed in words per minute (default 25).
Sets effective speed for spaces (Farnsworth spacing).
Adds background noise at an SNR from -10 to 10; negative values must be quoted.

brief.install_notes: Official downloads include a Windows EXE (with OGG/MP3 support), an MP3-only and an OGG-only EXE, a static Linux binary, and source tarballs for the program and GUI. Packages exist for Debian, Ubuntu (PPA ppa:kamalmostafa/ebook2cw), FreeBSD ports, and ArchLinux, and the Mac OS X build is described in separate instructions. On Windows, ebook2cw.conf and map files go in the same folder as the executable; on Linux they are also read from ~/.ebook2cw/. The GUI needs ebook2cw.exe saved alongside it or on the executable path.
brief.standout: It is a text-to-Morse converter that writes ordinary MP3 or OGG files and can be built as a CGI, which the Learn CW Online site uses to generate Morse on demand. Character mapping lets accented letters be sent as simpler Morse equivalents, and inline commands change speed or pitch mid-text.
brief.status: Maintained. ebook2cw 0.8.5 was released 16 Aug 2023, and the homepage was last modified 21 Apr 2024. The GUI, ebook2cwgui 0.1.2, dates from January 2013. I did not check the git repository's commit history.
brief.caveats: Input must be plain text (ASCII, ISO 8859-1 or UTF-8), so ebooks in other formats need converting first; the homepage does not say which formats are accepted. UTF-8 support covers Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew and Arabic only, and mapping of multi-byte UTF-8 is limited. The GUI was designed for Windows 95 through 7, and its Mac OS X support is marked not tested. The author notes copyright varies by country and points to public-domain sources such as Project Gutenberg. The software is GPLv2.
quotes: ebook2cw is a command line program (optional graphical user interface available) which converts a plain text (ASCII, ISO 8859-1 or UTF-8) file (e. g. an ebook) to Morse code MP3 or OGG audio files.
The author claims no credit for the original idea to convert books to morse.
Of course ebook2cw is free software (free as in beer and free as in freedom) and published under the GPLv2.

entry.title: ebook2cw
entry.tldr: Turns a plain text file into Morse code audio, MP3 or OGG, so you can listen to a whole book sent in CW at the speed you choose.
entry.deeper_look:
ebook2cw reads a text file (ASCII, ISO 8859-1 or UTF-8) and writes Morse code audio files. You choose the speed, tone frequency, waveform and bitrate. It can split the output into numbered files at chapter markers, or by duration or word count, and it can add ID3 tags so the result behaves like an audiobook on a player.

It was written by Fabian Kurz (DJ5CW, formerly DJ1YFK) so that anyone could make a CW audiobook to their own liking. Earlier hams had already made Morse audiobooks, but shipping finished audio files was inflexible and used a lot of bandwidth. His answer was to distribute the converter and let people generate the audio themselves. The author "claims no credit for the original idea to convert books to morse."

Inline commands in the text change things mid-stream: `|f400` shifts the tone, `|w60` changes the speed, `|S1000` inserts silence, and prosigns can be written like `<AR>`. There is also Farnsworth spacing, which sends characters fast but stretches the gaps, a common way to learn Morse. It can mix in background noise at a chosen signal-to-noise ratio to simulate a real band.

The program can also be built as a CGI that returns a sound file from a URL. The Learn CW Online site uses this to generate Morse on demand.

entry.whats_unique: It writes ordinary MP3 or OGG files from whole books, with inline commands to change pitch and speed mid-text. It can also be built as a CGI that generates Morse on demand.
entry.caveats: Input must be plain text, so ebooks in other formats need converting first; UTF-8 support covers only Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew and Arabic, and the optional GUI dates from 2013.
